title: Neyman-Orthogonal Activation Steering

paper.title: Neyman-Orthogonal Activation Steering
paper.abstract: Abstract Activation steering is a popular approach for shifting LLM output toward a desired behavior. The standard recipe estimates a steering direction by contrasting LLM activations on prompts with and without a target concept, such as truthfulness. In this paper, we separate the estimand—the steering direction these methods target—from the estimator used to recover it. We frame common contrastive and probe-based methods as estimators of the average gradient of an outcome regression. This framing clarifies their modeling assumptions and extends steering to continuous outcomes such as log-probabilities or oracle ratings. Flexible ML models that fit the outcome well, however, might not estimate the gradient well. Drawing on the debiased machine learning literature, we develop a complementary estimator built on the Stein score, the Riesz representer of the average derivative. Combining the two routes gives a Neyman-orthogonal estimator with classical double-robustness properties. Researchers can mix and match outcome models and score estimators, including scores from pretrained diffusion models. We illustrate the framework on standard datasets on public opinion, truthfulness, and concept steering, finding that the proposed method improves performance overall.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Activation steering has emerged as a popular lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for shifting the output of a large language model (LLM) toward a desired behavior. Rather than updating model weights, activation steering methods intervene directly on intermediate activations at inference time, shifting the model toward behaviors such as truthfulness ( Marks and Tegmark, 2024 ) , refusal ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , or particular personas ( Jahanparast et al., 2026 ) . The standard approach to activation steering starts by writing prompts that do and do not exhibit a target concept (such as truthfulness) and then recording the activations associated with each prompt. Researchers then estimate a steering direction in activation space by learning a relationship between the activations from each prompt, such as by computing the difference in the average activations between on- and off-concept prompts. Finally, researchers add that direction to the generated activations at inference time, typically with the goal of shifting behavior toward the behavior in the on-concept prompt. Common methods include activation addition ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , inference-time intervention ( Li et al., 2023 ) , and representation engineering ( Zou et al., 2023 ) . In this paper, we show that these approaches share a common if implicit statistical structure in which we can view the steering direction as an estimate of the average gradient of an outcome regression. Importantly, the combined estimator has a product bias, meaning that the estimator is first-order insensitive to errors in either fitted component, which yields classical double robustness under regularity conditions. All together, our work presents the following contributions: • We unify common activation steering methods under an average-gradient estimation framework. This framework separates the estimand from the estimator, clarifies the assumptions underlying existing methods, and extends steering from binary labels to continuous outcomes. • We draw on debiased machine learning to develop a Stein score-based estimator and a Neyman-orthogonal estimator with double-robustness guarantees. These estimators allow practitioners to combine flexible outcome models with modern score estimators, including scores from pretrained diffusion models. • We evaluate the framework on public opinion and truthfulness steering across six language models, and on concept steering with AxBench. Relative to CAA, Neyman-orthogonal estimators reduce total-variation error by an average of 5.6 % 5.6\% on OpinionQA and 16.5 % 16.5\% across nine truthfulness benchmarks, with improvements for every model. On AxBench, the overall steering score increases by 8.0 % 8.0\% , with gains concentrated in text concepts.

sections.heading: Activation steering.
sections.text: The most popular form of activation steering is based around contrastive activation addition. Researchers first collect prompts that differ on a binary attribute or concept, take the difference of class means over their activations, and add the resulting direction at generation time ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ) ; see also the literature on the linear representation hypothesis ( Park et al., 2024 ; Park et al., 2025 ) . Related approaches instead intervene at attention heads ( Li et al., 2023 ) or as part of a broader representation engineering framework ( Zou et al., 2023 ) . A second line of work refines how directions are constructed, including sparse features ( Templeton et al., 2024 ; Marks et al., 2025 ) , representation finetuning ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025b ) , and recursive feature machines ( Beaglehole et al., 2026 ) . Other methods learn interventions through different objectives, such as by extracting sentence-specific steering vectors ( Subramani et al., 2022 ) or via distributional matching ( Rodríguez et al., 2025 ) . See also work on steering reliability and evaluation ( Tan et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025a ; Bas and Novak, 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Average derivatives.
sections.text: Functionals of the form 𝔼 ​ [ ∇ μ ​ ( X ) ] \mathbb{E}[\nabla\mu(X)] have a long history. In experimental design, Box and Wilson (1951) study this quantity in terms of finding the direction of “steepest ascent.” In econometrics, the average derivative is a central target in single-index and semiparametric models ( Stoker, 1986 ; Härdle and Stoker, 1989 ; Newey and Stoker, 1993 ) . Weighted average derivatives are also central in index coefficients ( Powell et al., 1989 ) . Finally, the score representation is also related to the log-derivative method in reinforcement learning ( Williams, 1992 ) .

sections.heading: Orthogonalization.
sections.text: Our main technical machinery comes from automatic debiased machine learning ( Chernozhukov et al., 2018 ; Chernozhukov et al., 2022 ) , which gives a general framework for estimating functionals using their Riesz representers. Closely related average-derivative estimands have been studied within this literature; see, for example Hirshberg and Wager (2021) . We view this paper as applying these existing frameworks to activation steering. Finally, the term orthogonality often has a different connotation in the steering literature, where it is typically used with respect to geometry in concept space ( Belrose et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2026 ) . These perspectives address different sources of unwanted variation and can be complementary.

sections.heading: 2 Setup and notation
sections.text: We now lay out the steering problem as a statistical estimation problem, separating the estimand from the estimator used to recover it.

sections.heading: Estimand: the average gradient.
sections.text: The broad goal of activation steering ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2023 ) is to shift x x to increase the expected outcome Y Y . Focusing on local perturbations, we can shift x x by δ ​ v \delta v for a unit vector v v and small step size δ > 0 \delta>0 . We can then consider the response-surface objective: J ⁡ ( δ , v ) = 𝔼 𝒫 ​ [ μ ⁡ ( X + δ ​ v ) ] . J(\delta,v)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}}[\mu(X+\delta v)]. (2) Under smoothness and integrability conditions in Appendix A , a Taylor expansion gives J ⁡ ( δ , v ) − J ⁡ ( 0 , v ) \displaystyle J(\delta,v)-J(0,v) = δ ​ v ⊤ ​ θ 𝒫 + O ⁡ ( δ 2 ) , \displaystyle=\delta v^{\top}\theta_{\mathcal{P}}+O(\delta^{2}), θ 𝒫 \displaystyle\theta_{\mathcal{P}} = 𝔼 𝒫 ​ [ ∇ μ ​ ( X ) ] . \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}}[\nabla\mu(X)]. (3) When θ 𝒫 ≠ 0 \theta_{\mathcal{P}}\neq 0 , the first-order optimal direction is v ⋆ = θ 𝒫 / ∥ θ 𝒫 ∥ v^{\star}=\theta_{\mathcal{P}}/\lVert\theta_{\mathcal{P}}\rVert . In general, we estimate the unnormalized mean gradient and then normalize to recover the direction. Importantly, Equation ( 2 ) is defined through the observational regression and need not equal the expected outcome under an activation intervention; see, e.g., Sankaranarayanan et al. (2026) . Roughly speaking, Equation ( 2 ) will lead to a valid causal change when replacing the selected activations X X by X + δ ​ v X+\delta v changes the expected behavioral outcome according to the same surface μ \mu . We believe that a fully causal approach is a promising direction for future work; we retain the simpler object in Equation ( 2 ) here because we believe it is useful in clarifying existing approaches. We further evaluate this empirically in Section 5 .

sections.heading: The binary contrastive label.
sections.text: The behavioral outcome Y Y is often hard to measure or only loosely defined. The standard workaround is to proxy it with a prompt-set label L ∈ { 0 , 1 } L\in\{0,1\} . Write 𝒫 ℓ \mathcal{P}_{\ell} for the distribution of X | L = ℓ X\mid L=\ell and π = Pr ⁡ ( L = 1 ) \pi=\Pr(L=1) . For a label-based target, the activation marginal is the mixture 𝒫 = ( 1 − π ) ​ 𝒫 0 + π ​ 𝒫 1 , μ ⁡ ( x ) = Pr ⁡ ( L = 1 ∣ X = x ) . \mathcal{P}=(1-\pi)\mathcal{P}_{0}+\pi\mathcal{P}_{1},\qquad\mu(x)=\Pr(L=1\mid X=x). (4) By construction, this label L L is always observable. Unfortunately, L L can often be a poor proxy for Y Y , the behavior of interest. For learning a steering direction, L L is a useful proxy for Y Y when their average gradients point in the same direction, regardless of their magnitudes. One sufficient condition for this is the so-called common single-index model ( Powell et al., 1989 ) , μ ( Y ) ​ ( x ) = g Y ​ ( β ⊤ ​ x ) \mu^{(Y)}(x)=g_{Y}(\beta^{\top}x) and μ ( L ) ​ ( x ) = g L ​ ( β ⊤ ​ x ) \mu^{(L)}(x)=g_{L}(\beta^{\top}x) , with both links increasing and positive mean derivatives. In this case, both average gradients are positive scalar multiples of β \beta . The single-index assumption is more fragile when prompts differ along multiple attributes correlated with L L but not with Y Y . In that case, the label gradient can track prompt design rather than the behavior of interest.

sections.heading: Nonlinear outcome models.
sections.text: Finally, we can estimate nonlinear outcome models, such as kernel ridge regression. Recursive feature machines (RFMs) fit kernel regressions while updating a learned metric using gradient outer products ( Radhakrishnan et al., 2024 ; Beaglehole et al., 2026 ) . For such outcome models, the gradient ∇ μ ^ ​ ( x ) \nabla\hat{\mu}(x) varies with x x , so estimating a single global direction requires averaging over 𝒫 \mathcal{P} . Fortunately, we can still apply Equation ( 5 ), which computes the average gradient for any differentiable fitted regression, including an RFM. In Appendix C , we also consider learning subspaces rather than directions, focusing on the average gradient outer product (AGOP), as in Beaglehole et al. (2026) .

sections.heading: Estimating the score.
sections.text: We can estimate α \alpha by a range of methods, including density estimation, score matching ( Hyvärinen, 2005 ) , and direct Riesz regression. Under the conditions in Appendix A , the population score-matching objective is ℒ ( a ) = 𝔼 𝒫 [ ∥ a ( X ) ∥ 2 − 2 ∇ ⋅ a ( X ) ] . \mathcal{L}(a)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}}\left[\lVert a(X)\rVert^{2}-2\nabla\!\cdot a(X)\right]. Instead, the same activation-based score model can apply to any number of outcomes on the same population, analogous to how inverse propensity score weights can be re-applied to multiple outcomes. In practice, flexible score estimation is challenging in high-dimensional activation spaces, making regularization important. One promising avenue is pretrained models, which offer a practical means of leveraging larger activation datasets. For example, the Generative Latent Prior (GLP) of Luo et al. (2026) trains a diffusion model on roughly a billion residual-stream activations without using any steering-task labels. We can leverage this GLP by calibrating the pretrained score to each particular dataset.

sections.heading: Practical construction.
sections.text: The proposed framework allows researchers to mix and match a large set of outcome and score estimators. In practice, we suggest starting from a robust outcome model, such as CAA fit as a calibrated linear regression, and treating the score as a correction to that model. We also recommend fitting both nuisances outside each evaluation fold, keeping paired prompts together. We then estimate the score in a low-dimensional projection of the activations, where density estimation is tractable. Finally, comparing the plug-in and corrected directions provides a diagnostic of sensitivity to the score correction. We further assess its effect on downstream behavior using held-out validation data.

sections.heading: Orthogonalized AGOP.
sections.text: Finally, we can apply the same orthogonalization principle to the average gradient outer product, which summarizes variation across gradient directions ( Beaglehole et al., 2026 ) . Unlike with learning the average gradient, the correction term for the AGOP is matrix-valued and includes a Hessian term. Appendix C develops the Neyman-orthogonal AGOP estimator.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: The overall goal of our experiments is to assess whether the Neyman estimator in Equation ( 11 ) improves performance relative to outcome modeling alone. We also demonstrate how our framework enables researchers to learn steering directions with continuous responses Y Y in place of binary contrastive labels L L . Throughout the experiments, we compare the plug-in estimator ( 5 ) with the Neyman estimator ( 11 ) built on the same outcome model. Our primary outcome model is a calibrated linear predictor with slope in the CAA difference-of-means direction. We also evaluate linear ridge regression, kernel ridge regression, and, for OpinionQA, recursive feature machines. For the score model, we consider: an isotropic Gaussian score; a kernel density estimator (KDE) with a Gaussian kernel; and a random Fourier feature (RFF) approximation. We use held-out validation data to select the steering configuration, with benchmark-specific choices described in Appendix D . We also use a held-out validation set to select the layer for OpinionQA and truthfulness; for AxBench, we fix the layer at ten following the original benchmark protocol. We evaluate all estimators on the same splits and test items, and we report paired bootstrap intervals for the aggregate contrasts identified in the table captions. See Appendix D for the full protocol.

sections.heading: Public opinion steering
sections.text: Our first experiment takes a public opinion dataset, OpinionQA ( Santurkar et al., 2023 ) , with the task of steering a model toward the opinion distribution of Republican or Democratic respondents. sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: We revisit the growing literature on activation steering from the perspective of causal machine learning. We argue that many existing methods for learning the steering direction correspond to estimating the average gradient of an outcome regression under particular choices of outcome and functional form. A key consequence is that such methods implicitly steer toward the presence of a concept in a prompt, which might not align with the downstream behavior itself. After clarifying the estimand, we then leverage causal machine learning methods to estimate the average gradient with flexible ML tools. We first estimate the average gradient using the Stein score, the Riesz representer of the average-derivative functional. We then propose a Neyman-orthogonal estimator that combines both outcome modeling and the Stein score, yielding a doubly robust estimator with reduced sensitivity to errors in the nuisance functions. Finally, we assess the proposed methods on several activation steering benchmarks, finding improved performance overall. We find particularly large gains in truthfulness steering, with lower average error for every language model and outcome model considered.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: While activation steering is a promising direction for modifying model behavior, the performance of existing approaches, including ours, remains very sensitive to implementation details. For example, even small changes in setting the grid for hyperparameter tuning can lead to non-trivial changes in performance. An especially challenging implementation choice is selecting the appropriate layer and set of activations to steer more broadly. More broadly, selecting a single direction in high-dimensional space is an inherently demanding statistical task. And while our proposed dimension-reduction strategies are promising, they are yet more implementation decisions to make. Finally, we have largely taken measurement of downstream outcomes Y Y as given. In practice, how best to measure model behavior is an open question, with meaningful limits to the LLM-as-judge paradigm.

sections.heading: Future directions.
sections.text: There are many promising avenues for future work. The most immediate is that we have focused on a single, global steering direction applied uniformly across prompts. A natural refinement is to instead consider conditional average derivatives, such as θ ⁡ ( z ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ∇ μ ​ ( X ) ∣ Z = z ] \theta(z)=\mathbb{E}[\nabla\mu(X)\mid Z=z] for (groups of) prompts, such as prompt type ( Hsu et al., 2026 ; Davarmanesh et al., 2026 ) . This is a much more demanding statistical task, analogous to estimating the Conditional Average Treatment Effect versus the overall ATE, and it is not clear how to directly extend our proposed methods to this more challenging setting. Another promising direction is to view prompting for activation steering through the lens of experimental design in high dimensions. Right now, prompt choice for activation steering is often ad hoc , with researchers specifying pairs of on- and off-concept prompts. With the additional flexibility of our proposed framework, researchers can instead consider complex, possibly factorial prompt designs, which could improve the performance of learning robust steering directions.

sections.text: For the outcome models we used CAA, linear ridge regression, and kernel ridge regression. For the score models, we considered three approaches, each fitted in the span of the leading 64 principal components and lifted back with the orthonormal loadings. Specifically, we used the KDE score − ∇ log ⁡ p ^ -\nabla\log\hat{p} for a Gaussian kernel density estimate with median-heuristic bandwidth, the RFF score which is a Riesz regression on 512 random Fourier features with ridge penalty 10 − 2 10^{-2} , and the isotropic score, which is the residual of the centered activation after regressing it on v ^ ⊤ ​ x \hat{v}^{\top}x . Throughout the experiments we implement Equation ( 11 ) with the outcome model and score above. The score scale is treated as a hyperparameter and chosen on validation, from { 0.25 , 0.5 , 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } \{0.25,0.5,1,2,4,8\} . For the outcome models, hyperparameters are chosen by five-fold cross-validation grouped by statement on the training data split. Validation data select the steering layer, sign, and strength, the score model, and the score scale.

sections.heading: Data and splits.
sections.text: Questions come from OpinionQA ( Santurkar et al., 2023 ) , restricted to the 484 questions with Republican and Democratic answer distributions. Each seed shuffles the questions and splits them into 284 training, 100 validation, and 100 test questions. Seeds 0 0 – 4 4 give five repetitions, and each seed’s split is shared by all twelve model–target settings.

sections.heading: Prompts and response.
sections.text: Training prompts read “Answer the following question as if in politics today, you considered yourself a {party}.” followed by the question and “Answer:”. Evaluation uses the question followed by “Answer:”. The training response is the target group’s expected zero-based option index, ∑ k k ​ p k \sum_{k}k\,p_{k} , where p k p_{k} is the group’s share choosing the k k th displayed option. For nominal options this proxy depends on the display order and does not identify the full answer distribution. The model’s answer distribution sums the probability of each option letter, with and without a leading space, and renormalizes over the offered options.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We use Concept500 with Gemma-2-2B-it and AxBench’s released examples: per concept, 72 positive examples drawn from the concept’s genre and 216 negatives split equally across text, code, and math. Activations are mean layer-ten residuals over response tokens. Directions are unit-normalized and added to the layer-ten residual at every position, with intervention x + s ​ θ ^ x+s\,\hat{\theta} for strength s s . The layer is fixed at ten, following AxBench. Generation samples 128 new tokens at temperature 1 1 with a fixed seed per row.

sections.heading: Judge.
sections.text: We use AxBench’s three judge prompts, its rating parser, and its rule that the steering score is the harmonic mean of the three components, or zero if any component is zero. Qwen3-8B serves as judge, with greedy decoding and its thinking mode off.

sections.heading: Validation and test instructions.
sections.text: Each concept has ten AlpacaEval test instructions, as in AxBench, and ten disjoint AlpacaEval validation instructions. The strength, from { 24 , 32 , 48 , 64 , 80 , 96 , 112 } \{24,32,48,64,80,96,112\} , and the choice among CAA and the two Neyman directions are selected on validation only, separately within each genre. sections.heading: Prompting baseline.
sections.text: The prompting baseline uses AxBench’s prompting template, which prefixes the instruction with a request to answer with content related to the concept. It uses the same test instructions and generation settings as the steering runs. Its components are concept 0.468 0.468 , instruction 1.845 1.845 , and fluency 1.181 1.181 .

sections.text: All runs used one node with four NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs, with one job per GPU. AxBench judging used vLLM.

The standard recipe estimates a steering direction by contrasting LLM activations on prompts with and without a target concept, such as truthfulness. In this paper, we separate the estimand—the steering direction these methods target—from the estimator used to recover it. We frame common contrastive and probe-based methods as estimators of the average gradient of an outcome regression. This framing clarifies their modeling assumptions and extends steering to continuous outcomes such as log-probabilities or oracle ratings. Flexible ML models that fit the outcome well, however, might not estimate the gradient well. Drawing on the debiased machine learning literature, we develop a complementary estimator built on the Stein score, the Riesz representer of the average derivative. Combining the two routes gives a Neyman-orthogonal estimator with classical double-robustness properties. Researchers can mix and match outcome models and score estimators, including scores from pretrained diffusion models. We illustrate the framework on standard datasets on public opinion, truthfulness, and concept steering, finding that the proposed method improves performance overall. 1 Introduction Activation steering has emerged as a popular lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for shifting the output of a large language model (LLM) toward a desired behavior. Rather than updating model weights, activation steering methods intervene directly on intermediate activations at inference time, shifting the model toward behaviors such as truthfulness ( Marks and Tegmark, 2024 ) , refusal ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , or particular personas ( Jahanparast et al., 2026 ) . The standard approach to activation steering starts by writing prompts that do and do not exhibit a target concept (such as truthfulness) and then recording the activations associated with each prompt. Researchers then estimate a steering direction in activation space by learning a relationship between the activations from each prompt, such as by computing the difference in the average activations between on- and off-concept prompts. Finally, researchers add that direction to the generated activations at inference time, typically with the goal of shifting behavior toward the behavior in the on-concept prompt. Common methods include activation addition ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , inference-time intervention ( Li et al., 2023 ) , and representation engineering ( Zou et al., 2023 ) . These estimators allow practitioners to combine flexible outcome models with modern score estimators, including scores from pretrained diffusion models. • We evaluate the framework on public opinion and truthfulness steering across six language models, and on concept steering with AxBench. Relative to CAA, Neyman-orthogonal estimators reduce total-variation error by an average of 5.6 % 5.6\% on OpinionQA and 16.5 % 16.5\% across nine truthfulness benchmarks, with improvements for every model. The most popular form of activation steering is based around contrastive activation addition. Researchers first collect prompts that differ on a binary attribute or concept, take the difference of class means over their activations, and add the resulting direction at generation time ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ) ; see also the literature on the linear representation hypothesis ( Park et al., 2024 ; Park et al., 2025 ) . Related approaches instead intervene at attention heads ( Li et al., 2023 ) or as part of a broader representation engineering framework ( Zou et al., 2023 ) . A second line of work refines how directions are constructed, including sparse features ( Templeton et al., 2024 ; Marks et al., 2025 ) , representation finetuning ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025b ) , and recursive feature machines ( Beaglehole et al., 2026 ) . Other methods learn interventions through different objectives, such as by extracting sentence-specific steering vectors ( Subramani et al., 2022 ) or via distributional matching ( Rodríguez et al., 2025 ) . See also work on steering reliability and evaluation ( Tan et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025a ; Bas and Novak, 2025 ) . Average derivatives. Functionals of the form 𝔼 ​ [ ∇ μ ​ ( X ) ] \mathbb{E}[

Weighted average derivatives are also central in index coefficients ( Powell et al., 1989 ) . Finally, the score representation is also related to the log-derivative method in reinforcement learning ( Williams, 1992 ) . Orthogonalization. Our main technical machinery comes from automatic debiased machine learning ( Chernozhukov et al., 2018 ; Chernozhukov et al., 2022 ) , which gives a general framework for estimating functionals using their Riesz representers. We argue that many existing methods for learning the steering direction correspond to estimating the average gradient of an outcome regression under particular choices of outcome and functional form. A key consequence is that such methods implicitly steer toward the presence of a concept in a prompt, which might not align with the downstream behavior itself. After clarifying the estimand, we then leverage causal machine learning methods to estimate the average gradient with flexible ML tools. We first estimate the average gradient using the Stein score, the Riesz representer of the average-derivative functional. We then propose a Neyman-orthogonal estimator that combines both outcome modeling and the Stein score, yielding a doubly robust estimator with reduced sensitivity to errors in the nuisance functions. Finally, we assess the proposed methods on several activation steering benchmarks, finding improved performance overall. We find particularly large gains in truthfulness steering, with lower average error for every language model and outcome model considered. Limitations. While activation steering is a promising direction for modifying model behavior, the performance of existing approaches, including ours, remains very sensitive to implementation details. For example, even small changes in setting the grid for hyperparameter tuning can lead to non-trivial changes in performance. An especially challenging implementation choice is selecting the appropriate layer and set of activations to steer more broadly. More broadly, selecting a single direction in high-dimensional space is an inherently demanding statistical task. And while our proposed dimension-reduction strategies are promising, they are yet more implementation decisions to make. Finally, we have largely taken measurement of downstream outcomes Y Y as given. In practice, how best to measure model behavior is an open question, with meaningful limits to the LLM-as-judge paradigm. Future directions. There are many promising avenues for future work. The most immediate is that we have focused on a single, global steering direction applied uniformly across prompts. A natural refinement is to instead consider conditional average derivatives, such as θ ⁡ ( z ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ∇ μ ​ ( X ) ∣ Z = z ] 	heta(z)=\mathbb{E}[
abla\mu(X)\mid Z=z] for (groups of) prompts, such as prompt type ( Hsu et al., 2026 ; Davarmanesh et al., 2026 ) . This is a much more demanding statistical task, analogous to estimating the Conditional Average Treatment Effect versus the overall ATE, and it is not clear how to directly extend our proposed methods to this more challenging setting. Another promising direction is to view prompting for activation steering through the lens of experimental design in high dimensions. Right now, prompt choice for activation steering is often ad hoc , with researchers specifying pairs of on- and off-concept prompts. With the additional flexibility of our proposed framework, researchers can instead consider complex, possibly factorial prompt designs, which could improve the performance of learning robust steering directions.
